Mitigate

/MIT-ih-gayt/ - the stress falls on MIT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Mitigate means to make something less severe or harmful.

Rubber pads under the printing press mitigated the vibration that had been cracking the shop's old plaster.

Worked Example

Nothing would stop the freight line from running behind the new apartments, so the builders set out to mitigate the noise: triple-glazed windows facing the tracks, bedrooms placed on the far side, and a spruce-planted berm between the rails and the courtyard. Tenants sleep through the 3 a.m. coal train.

Mitigate is the precise verb because it means to make something less severe or harmful — the train still comes, at full volume, but its effect on the tenants is softened. Prevent would be false, and alleviate would point at the tenants' discomfort; mitigate aims at the harm itself.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lessen: Lessen is plain arithmetic: any amount can lessen — costs, noise, attendance — with no hint of harm in it. Mitigate is aimed: it takes something harmful, flood risk or damage or a penalty, and dials its severity down while the thing itself keeps existing.

dampen: To dampen is to deaden force or liveliness the way a wet cloth deadens sound — vibration, enthusiasm, a market rally. Mitigate is the planner's word for cutting a harm's severity; dampen needs no harm at all and can act on perfectly healthy energy.

temper: To temper something is to moderate it by blending in a counterweight — justice tempered with mercy, criticism tempered with encouragement. Mitigate simply cuts how severe a harm is; temper changes the mix, folding a softening element into the thing rather than shrinking the harm itself.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

heighten: to sharpen the harm instead of softening it

worsen: to leave the damage larger than you found it

Where it sits · how much of the harm is removed — soften → mitigate → cancel out

soften vs. mitigate: Softening is the lighter touch — it takes a bit of the sting out but stops short of mitigating, which meaningfully cuts the damage down.

cancel out vs. mitigate: Cancel out goes further than mitigate — mitigation leaves a reduced harm still standing, while canceling out erases the harm altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — mitig

Root — mitig: to make mild (Latin mitigare, from mitis, 'soft, mild')

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb: to make, to do

Put it together

Put it together: Mitig- (to make mild, from Latin mitis, 'soft') + -ate = to make mild. Romans used mitis for ripe fruit and gentle tempers — anything without hardness in it. English took only the verb: to mitigate a punishment, a risk, or a noise is to take the hardness out of it without pretending it is gone.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin mitis ('soft, mild') survives in English almost nowhere outside mitigate itself — no everyday cousin kept the root. The nearest thing is the word's own shadow: an unmitigated disaster is harm with nothing soft about it, the root's meaning read in reverse.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / technical

Mitigate is the planner's and lawyer's verb: it aims at the harmful thing itself — flood risk, noise, a sentence's severity — and dials its force down. Alleviate eases what the sufferer feels; palliate treats symptoms while the cause stays; ameliorate lifts a whole bad situation. When a report promises 'mitigation measures,' it means the hazard remains, made smaller.
